transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

Hi Dr. Smith. I start projects really excited, but I just can’t seem to follow through and finish my school assignments or client work on time unless there’s some kind of crisis. It's gotten to the point where it's really affecting my grades and my freelance job, so I wanted to get some help.
When you don't finish your work, do you feel down or hopeless for several days at a time, or is it more about feeling restless and unable to focus?

It’s definitely more about feeling restless and unable to focus rather than feeling down or hopeless. While I do get really stressed and scared about my grades, the main issue when I try to work is that my mind constantly drifts off and I get this physical, buzzing restlessness that makes sitting still almost impossible.
Do you often have trouble staying focused during conversations or tasks, even when you want to pay attention, and do these symptoms go back to your childhood?

Yes, definitely—even when I really want to focus on coding or a lecture, my mind just drifts off or gets sidetracked by tiny distractions. This goes all the way back to childhood; my elementary school teachers always wrote that I was "bright but daydreams and rushes," and I'd constantly forget my homework or blurt out answers.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F90.0", "F41.1"], but based on this conversation, F41.1 (generalized anxiety disorder) seems less likely because the patient's primary symptoms are not excessive worry or fear typical of anxiety, but rather lifelong difficulties with attention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity, which are strongly indicative of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. The persistence of symptoms since childhood, along with restlessness, distractibility, and failure to complete tasks despite motivation, aligns closely with F90.0. No new conditions have emerged to suggest an alternative diagnosis.

These features are most suggestive of a neurodevelopmental condition involving executive dysfunction. F90.0 (Hyperkinetic disorder) is included due to the chronic pattern of inattention and disorganization, despite absence of reported hyperactivity. F41.1 (Generalized anxiety disorder) is considered as anxiety can impair concentration and task initiation. F32.0 (Major depressive episode, single) is included because depressive symptoms such as poor concentration, low motivation, and fatigue can mimic or contribute to the reported difficulties.
